title: A new project
goal: Introduce yourself and others in a formal meeting, say in what capacity you are there and why, and move comfortably between the meeting-room register and the ordinary Indonesian you already speak.
bekal: introduce yourself and a colleague formally with *perkenalkan* and *selaku*
explain the purpose of a visit with *dalam rangka* and *terkait*
interrupt, ask and thank politely in a meeting: *mohon maaf, izin bertanya*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Pertemuan pertama di balai desa
dialogs.intro: February 2028, a Thursday morning. In the village hall of Sumberwangi, a few kilometres from Borobudur, the head of the village opens the first meeting about the new tourism project. Sarah is the guest.

lines.speaker: Harun:
lines.text: Bapak-Ibu sekalian, selamat pagi. Mari kita mulai pertemuan hari ini.
lines.id: Good morning, everyone. Let's begin today's meeting.
lines.literal: Sir-Madam all, good morning. let us begin meeting day this.

lines.speaker: Ratna:
lines.text: Semua sudah hadir, Pak Kades. Tamu dari Yogya juga sudah datang.
lines.id: Everyone's here, Pak Kades. Our guest from Yogya has arrived too.
lines.literal: all already present, Mr Village-Head. guest from Yogya also already come.

lines.speaker: Harun:
lines.text: Baik. Perkenalkan, ini Mbak Sarah, koordinator program desa wisata kita.
lines.id: Good. Allow me to introduce Mbak Sarah, the coordinator of our tourism-village programme.
lines.literal: good. introduce, this Miss Sarah, coordinator programme village tourism our.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Terima kasih, Pak. Selamat pagi, Bapak-Ibu. Perkenalkan, nama saya Sarah, dari Australia.
lines.id: Thank you, sir. Good morning, everyone. Let me introduce myself: my name is Sarah, from Australia.
lines.literal: thank you, Sir. good morning, Sir-Madam. introduce, name my Sarah, from Australia.

lines.speaker: Ratna:
lines.text: Wah, bahasa Indonesianya lancar sekali, Mbak.
lines.id: Wow, your Indonesian is really fluent.
lines.literal: wow, language Indonesian-her fluent very, Miss.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Terima kasih, Bu, saya masih belajar. Saya hadir di sini selaku koordinator dari kantor kami di Yogyakarta.
lines.id: Thank you, I'm still learning. I'm here in my capacity as coordinator for our office in Yogyakarta.
lines.literal: thank you, Madam, I still learn. I present at here as coordinator from office our in Yogyakarta.

lines.speaker: Harun:
lines.text: Mbak Sarah datang dalam rangka kerja sama antara kantornya, UGM, dan desa kita.
lines.id: Mbak Sarah is here as part of a partnership between her office, UGM and our village.
lines.literal: Miss Sarah come in framework work together between office-her, UGM, and village our.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Betul, Pak. Kami ingin mengembangkan Sumberwangi menjadi desa wisata bersama warga.
lines.id: That's right. We want to develop Sumberwangi into a tourism village together with the residents.

lines.speaker: Ratna:
lines.text: Mohon maaf, Mbak, izin bertanya. Nanti warga dapat apa?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Pertanyaan yang bagus, Bu. Homestay dan warung nanti dikelola langsung oleh warga.
lines.id: Good question. The homestays and food stalls will be run directly by the residents.

lines.speaker: Harun:
lines.text: Jadi keuntungannya untuk warga sendiri, bukan untuk orang luar.
lines.id: So the profit goes to the villagers themselves, not to outsiders.

lines.speaker: Ratna:
lines.text: Kalau begitu, kelompok ibu-ibu homestay siap membantu.
lines.id: In that case, the homestay women's group is ready to help.
lines.literal: if like-that, group mothers homestay ready help.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Terima kasih banyak, Bu. Minggu depan kami juga akan mengundang Dr. Lestari dari UGM.
lines.id: Thank you very much. Next week we'll also be inviting Dr. Lestari from UGM.
lines.literal: thank you much, Madam. week front we also will invite Dr. Lestari from UGM.

lines.speaker: Harun:
lines.text: Baik. Kita sepakati dulu: pertemuan rutin setiap Kamis malam di balai ini.

lines.speaker: Ratna:
lines.text: Setuju, Pak. Asal ada teh manis dan gorengan.
lines.id: Agreed. As long as there's sweet tea and fritters.
lines.literal: agree, Sir. as-long-as there-is tea sweet and fried-things.

notes: **Bapak-Ibu sekalian** is how you address a mixed group in any formal setting: "ladies and gentlemen, everyone". *Sekalian* here means "all of you together". On a stage you will also hear *hadirin* (those present) and *Bapak dan Ibu yang saya hormati*, which Unit 13 takes further.

**Pak Kades, balai desa, warga.** *Kades* is short for *kepala desa*, the elected head of the village, and Indonesians love these clipped official words (*Kadus, Sekdes, Pemda*). The *balai desa* is the village hall, and *warga* are the residents: the word the whole project is built around.

**Perkenalkan** is the formal "allow me to introduce". Pak Harun uses it for Sarah; Sarah uses it for herself. It is technically a command ("introduce!"), but nobody hears it that way; it works like a fixed announcement. Among friends the shorter *kenalin* does the same job.

**Saya masih belajar.** When someone praises your Indonesian, the expected answer is modest: "I'm still learning", or *ah, biasa saja* (oh, it's nothing special). Accepting the compliment with a plain *terima kasih* is fine too, but adding the modesty sounds much warmer.

**Mohon maaf, izin bertanya.** This is the polite way to break into a formal conversation: "begging your pardon, permission to ask". *Izin* (permission) turns up everywhere in official life: *izin, Pak* before you speak, leave, or even pass in front of someone. Among friends you just ask.

**Asal ada teh manis dan gorengan.** *Asal* means "as long as, provided that". Bu Ratna's joke is also a fact of village life: no evening meeting in Java happens without *teh manis* and a plate of *gorengan* (fried snacks: tofu, tempe, battered vegetables).

grammars.title: Introductions from casual to formal
body: You already know *Nama saya Sarah*. At B1 you need the whole ladder, because the same act of introducing sounds very different in a café, an office and a village hall.
after: In a formal introduction your **role** matters more than your hobbies. Indonesians expect name, institution, and position, in that order: *Nama saya Sarah, dari kantor Linguo Yogyakarta, selaku koordinator program.*
💬 *Kenalin* is the Jakarta *-in* form of *kenalkan*, which you met in A2. In Central Java you will hear the same casual *kenalin* from young people.

grammars.title: The meeting-room connectors
body: A handful of formal words carry most official talk. None is difficult; each simply replaces a plainer word you already know.
after: *Dalam rangka* is the one you will hear every week. Banners say *Dalam Rangka HUT RI ke-83* (celebrating Indonesia's 83rd Independence Day), letters say *dalam rangka kunjungan kerja* (on a working visit). It links an activity to its occasion or purpose.
⚠️ *Selaku* is only for a role you hold officially. *Selaku orang Australia* sounds odd; say *sebagai orang Australia*.

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Di ruang dosen, UGM
dialogs.intro: The following Monday. Sarah visits Dr. Lestari Wibowo in her office at Universitas Gadjah Mada in Yogyakarta to agree on the university's role.

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Silakan masuk, Mbak Sarah. Silakan duduk.
lines.id: Please come in, Mbak Sarah. Have a seat.
lines.literal: please enter, Miss Sarah. please sit.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Terima kasih, Bu. Mohon maaf saya agak terlambat. Jalan Kaliurang macet sekali.
lines.id: Thank you. I'm sorry I'm a little late. Jalan Kaliurang was terribly jammed.
lines.literal: thank you, Madam. beg sorry I rather late. road Kaliurang jammed very.

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Tidak apa-apa. Bagaimana pertemuan pertama di Sumberwangi?
lines.id: Not at all. How did the first meeting in Sumberwangi go?
lines.literal: not what-what. how meeting first in Sumberwangi?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Lancar, Bu. Warga cukup antusias, terutama kelompok homestay Bu Ratna.
lines.id: It went smoothly. The residents were quite keen, especially Bu Ratna's homestay group.
lines.literal: smooth, Madam. residents quite enthusiastic, especially group homestay Mrs Ratna.

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Syukurlah. Dari pihak UGM, kami akan mengirim tiga mahasiswa magang.
lines.id: Thank goodness. On UGM's side, we'll be sending three student interns.
lines.literal: thank-God. from side UGM, we will send three student intern.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Wah, bagus sekali. Mereka dari jurusan apa, Bu?
lines.id: Oh, that's great. What are they studying?
lines.literal: wow, good very. they from department what, Madam?

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Pariwisata dan antropologi. Salah satunya Yoga, anaknya aktif sekali di media sosial.
lines.id: Tourism and anthropology. One of them is Yoga, a very active lad on social media.
lines.literal: tourism and anthropology. wrong one-of-them Yoga, child-the active very at media social.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Kebetulan kami memang butuh orang seperti itu. Kapan mereka bisa mulai?
lines.id: As it happens, that's exactly the kind of person we need. When can they start?
lines.literal: by-chance we indeed need person like that. when they can start?

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Minggu depan. Tetapi sebelumnya kita perlu menandatangani nota kesepahaman.
lines.id: Next week. But before that we need to sign a memorandum of understanding.
lines.literal: week front. but before-it we need sign note mutual-understanding.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Baik, Bu. Draf MoU-nya akan saya kirim lewat surel paling lambat hari Jumat.
lines.id: Certainly. I'll send you the draft MoU by email by Friday at the latest.
lines.literal: good, Madam. draft MoU-the will I send via e-mail most slow day Friday.

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Terima kasih. Saya tunggu, ya, Mbak.
lines.id: Thank you. I'll look out for it.
lines.literal: thank you. I wait, [ya], Miss.

notes: **Bu, not Dokter.** Dr. Lestari has a doctorate, and it appears on her door and her emails, but you address her as *Bu Lestari* or simply *Bu*. *Dokter* in speech means a medical doctor. Professors are *Prof.* in writing and often *Prof* in speech too.

**Pihak** means "side, party": *dari pihak UGM* (on UGM's side), *pihak desa* (the village side), *kedua belah pihak* (both parties). It makes any institution sound like a participant in a formal arrangement, which is why contracts and news reports are full of it.

**Salah satunya** — "one of them". It looks like "wrong one", but *salah satu* is the fixed phrase for "one of": *salah satu mahasiswa* (one of the students). ⚠️ Keep the noun singular after it in careful writing: *salah satu desa*, not *salah satu desa-desa*.

**Kebetulan** is "by chance, as it happens". Indonesians use it constantly to introduce a happy coincidence, or politely to steer the talk: *Kebetulan saya juga mau tanya...* (as it happens, I also wanted to ask...).

**Surel** is the official word for email, built from *surat elektronik*. You will see it on forms and in government letters; in conversation almost everyone simply says *email* (pronounced *i-mél*). Sarah picks *surel* because she is being careful with an academic.
**Paling lambat** — "at the latest", literally "most slow". Its partner is *paling cepat* (at the earliest). Deadlines in Indonesian are almost always phrased this way: *paling lambat tanggal 15*.

grammars.title: Two registers of the same sentence
body: Dr. Lestari and Sarah speak standard Indonesian because the setting asks for it. Here is what the same content sounds like when two friends say it, and why you need both.

head: Standard (baku)
Everyday spoken
English
rows: We need to sign the MoU.

after: Notice that the gap is mostly in small words (*bagaimana/gimana, tidak/nggak*), the me- prefix (*mengirim/kirim*), and pronouns (*kami/kita, saya/aku*). The core vocabulary barely changes. That is good news: you are learning one language with two volume settings, not two languages.
💬 *Musti* is the spoken form of *mesti* (must). *Gapapa* is how *nggak apa-apa* looks in text messages.

sections.title: Who's who in an Indonesian village

blocks.text: A *desa* is a legal unit with its own elected head, budget and regulations. For a project like Sarah's, knowing who does what saves weeks. These are the people and bodies she will deal with in Sumberwangi.

head: Title or body
Short form
What they do
rows: runs the village office and paperwork
head of a hamlet within the village

blocks.text: Below the *dusun* come the RW and RT you met in Yogyakarta. You do not need to learn the long forms by heart, but you should recognise the short ones: people will say *Nanti tanya Pak Sekdes saja* as if everyone knows.
Formal meetings in Indonesia follow a reassuringly fixed script. Learn these lines as whole phrases; they are the scaffolding you hang your own sentences on.

head: Moment
Indonesian
English
rows: That concludes today's meeting. Thank you.

blocks.title: Good to know
items: *Atas* after *terima kasih* is the formal "for": *terima kasih atas perhatiannya*. In speech, *terima kasih untuk* is also fine.
*Demikian* (thus, so) closes meetings, letters and speeches. You will meet it again in B2 formal letters.
A village meeting often opens with *Assalamualaikum warahmatullahi wabarakatuh* and everyone answering *Waalaikumsalam*. Returning the greeting is polite whatever your own beliefs.
